claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by selective elemental segregation.
Selective segregation promotes a continuous, self-healing, adherent, nanostructured oxide scale.
Cr, Al, and Si are high-oxygen-affinity elements that segregate toward the surface under oxidizing conditions.
Preferential oxidation of surface-segregated Cr, Al, or Si limits oxygen ingress and further degradation.
The proposed initial alloy is homogeneous, near-equiatomic, and single-phase in the as-cast or homogenized state.
Systematically increasing oxide-forming-element content and segregation will produce different oxidation behavior than reducing their content.
Local chemical ordering and segregation at the oxide/alloy interface mediate formation of a nanostructured oxide layer.
The nanostructured oxide layer acts as a barrier that slows oxidation and helps preserve bulk integrity.
Preferential oxidation of segregated high-oxygen-affinity elements forms a dense and adherent mixed-oxide scale.
Local chemical ordering stabilizes the protective oxide scale.
High configurational entropy of the bulk alloy stabilizes the oxide scale by retarding oxygen and metal-ion diffusion.
Retarded oxygen and metal-ion diffusion limits oxide thickening, spallation, and subsequent material degradation.
Alloys engineered to promote selective oxidation will form thinner oxide scales than the baseline alloy.
Alloys engineered to promote selective oxidation will form more adherent and self-healing oxide scales than the baseline alloy.
The engineered alloys will exhibit lower oxide-scale growth rates and fewer microcracking or spallation events than the baseline.
The engineered alloys will retain mechanical integrity better during and after high-temperature oxidation than the baseline.
An alloy lacking tailored segregation will develop a more porous, discontinuous, or rapidly growing oxide scale and will degrade faster.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate at approximately 1000–1200 °C under oxidizing and cyclic-exposure conditions.
At sufficiently high temperatures or in sufficiently aggressive atmospheres, oxide-scale breakdown can render the proposed protective mechanism ineffective regardless of composition.
Failure of the optimized alloy to show a thinner, more coherent scale, lower oxidation kinetics, reduced spallation, and better mechanical retention than the control would falsify the hypothesis.
